entries.german: Ruprecht der Jüngste, Pfalzgraf bei Rhein, Herzog in Bayern urkundet, dass er mit Graf Johann von Wertheim überein gekommen ist, dass ihre Leute im Amt Lauda keine Todesfallabgabe entrichten sollen, bis auf Widerruf.
entries.english: Ruprecht the Younger, Count Palatine of the Rhine and Duke in Bavaria, records that he has reached an agreement with Count Johann of Wertheim that their people in the Lauda district are not to pay a death duty until further notice.
facts: Issued at Lauda ("Datum Luden") on the feast of St John the Baptist 1387, by Ruprecht III ("der Jüngste"), the later King Ruprecht, in person
Count Johann (Hans) von Wertheim is addressed as "unserm lieben Oheym"
The Palatinate and Wertheim held people in common ("gemeyner lute") in the Amt Lauda
These common people are to remain "unbeteilt", i.e. free of the "Teil" – the Franconian name for the death duty (Todfall/Besthaupt) – until revoked
The death duty was owed by a deceased bondsman's heirs to the lord: the best head of cattle, the best garment, or a share of the movable estate; paying it marked whose bondsman a person was
With two lords over the same people, both could claim the duty; the exemption removed a point of conflict between the Palatinate and Wertheim and burdened neither lord's subjects
Endorsement "Freibr." (Freibrief) shows the document was kept as a privilege of liberty
Lauda was a Palatine pledge from the Hohenlohe since 1376 (bought outright by the Palatinate in 1398)
Issued two days after Bishop Gerhard of Würzburg absolved the late Eberhard von Rosenberg, who had been killed by his mortal enemies near Lauda (GLA 43 Nr. 5662, 1387-06-22)
No mention of Eberhard von Rosenberg, his death, a feud or a reconciliation (Sühne); any connection is circumstantial
